text: Everyone watches price charts, refreshes the news, and follows the crowd's reactions. The more people react, the more people trade. The
entire system has made investing so frictionless that placing a buy order is almost as easy as clicking 'like.' And when
making a trade becomes that easy, the number of bad decisions tends to rise as well. Put those four factors together
and you get a very unusual environment. On one side, there is the pressure to make money fast. On the other
there is the feeling that the rules of the game are not entirely fair. In the middle, there are countless financial
tools promising to help people even the odds. When those conditions exist at the same time, the market inevitably creates products
to satisfy that demand. A striking example is the CFD scandal of 2023. CFD stands for 'contract for difference.' To put
it simply, a CFD allows you to speculate on whether an asset's price will go up or down without actually owning
the underlying asset. Like many other speculative products, CFDs often come with substantial leverage. And that can be extremely dangerous. According
to South Korean financial regulators, most of the people participating in CFD trading were actually individual investors. But in trading data
many of their transactions were recorded under the names of institutions or foreign investors. This distorted the market. Looking at
the data, it became difficult to tell who was actually buying, who was selling, and who was ultimately carrying the risk
When the scandal came to light, regulators responded in the familiar way: they introduced new rules, raised margin requirements, tightened eligibility
standards, and stepped up supervision. But those measures only addressed the symptoms. The underlying desire to speculate remained. Close one door
and people start looking for another. As CFDs came under tighter restrictions, money flowed into other leveraged products. Some of it
moved into overseas markets; some went into financial instruments that were more complicated and harder to supervise. By the end of
2024, South Korean individual investors had built up substantial holdings of foreign stocks. Among their investments, higher-risk products were becoming increasingly
common, including forms of leverage that were already restricted or tightly controlled at home. In other words, when people couldn't play
the game in their own backyard, they went looking for another field. This is why some experts compare speculation to flowing
